title: Benchmarking Coding Agents on New vs Legacy Codebases — Denys Linkov, Wisedocs

primary.label: Coding Agents & Software Engineering

domains.label: Coding Assistants

summary: Denys Linkov from Wisedocs audits the company's decision to refactor 10+ legacy medical claims processing repositories into a monorepo over six months. Wisedocs processes medical claims as PDFs exceeding 10,000 pages through ML pipelines. Three problems motivated the refactor: insufficient throughput for customer demand, excessive pipeline complexity, and developer aversion to legacy code. Linkov frames the decision against rapid AI coding tool improvements, citing Anthropic case studies from Spotify and Stripe showing AI-accelerated refactoring. He benchmarks a single Temporal-based refactor task across model generations: O3 took 3 hours with 10 major mistakes; Sonnet 4.6 needed one additional iteration; Opus 4.8 essentially one-shot the problem at roughly one-fifth original effort. He argues for reading METR task-length curves at 80-90% success rather than the standard 50%, since coin-flip odds on hour-long agent runs waste compute and attention. He warns of "AI psychosis"—trusting deep research reports that describe non-existent features. Testing GPT 5.5 extra high zero-shot, it declared completion in 10m22s writing 2,000 lines of scaffolding with models missing. Linkov estimates ~6 months until models consistently complete substantial refactors. He concludes the refactor was worthwhile: pipeline time and costs dropped, features that took months now ship in under a week, and developers company-wide volunteer into the repo. He cautions AI-native code risks becoming legacy-like without guardrails.
whyItMatters: The talk weaves together software engineering and AI concepts through a single decision: whether to refactor legacy code now or defer for better AI models. The monorepo refactor provides the concrete engineering context (tech debt compounding, feature parity verification, commit velocity as success metric, human PR reviews for context-building), while the AI benchmarking methodology and METR task-length curves provide the analytical framework for assessing whether deferring would have been viable. The zero-shot experiment (GPT 5.5 producing scaffolding only) and the AI psychosis warning demonstrate that AI capability assessments require critical verification—bridging AI evaluation with software engineering quality assurance. The tension between AI-native code becoming legacy-like and the human PR review process shows how AI tooling and engineering practices must co-evolve rather than substitute for each other. Plan mode adoption and agent harness evolution illustrate the incremental integration path. Together, these concepts form a practitioner's decision framework that is neither purely about software architecture nor purely about AI capability, but about the intersection where AI coding tools meet real-world engineering constraints and human governance.
temporalContext: This talk was published on August 8, 2026, with research conducted as of August 23, 2026. It references frontier AI models current as of mid-2026 (GPT 5.5 extra high, O3, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Opus 4.8) and cites the METR research paper from March 2025, Anthropic's Spotify case study from July 2025, Spotify's engineering blog from November 2025, and secondary corroboration of the Stripe case study from March 2026. The six-month Wisedocs monorepo refactor and the coding agent benchmarks reflect the state of AI coding tools and agent harnesses as of mid-2026, when plan mode had emerged in Claude Code and Cursor and sub-agent architectures were becoming standard in production development workflows.

concepts.name: Coding Agent Benchmarking Across Model Generations
concepts.explanation: Systematically comparing agent performance (iteration count, mistake rate, time-to-complete) on the same Temporal-based refactor task across different model versions: O3, Sonnet 4.6, Opus 4.8, and GPT 5.5 extra high.
concepts.importance: Provides the empirical foundation for the talk's claims about model improvement trajectories and the practical viability of AI-assisted refactoring at each capability level.

concepts.name: METR Task-Length Evaluation Framework
concepts.explanation: Research framework measuring the time horizon at which AI models complete tasks at given success rates, with the 50% horizon doubling roughly every seven months across 12 frontier models.
concepts.importance: Provides the external, research-validated methodology Linkov uses to assess when AI will be capable enough to defer refactors, grounding the decision framework in empirical trend data.

concepts.name: 80-90% Success Threshold for Agent Task Evaluation
concepts.explanation: Reading METR curves at 80-90% success rather than the standard 50%, arguing that launching hour-long agent runs on coin-flip odds wastes compute and developer attention.
concepts.importance: Offers a practical operational heuristic for teams deciding when to trust agent autonomy, shifting the decision threshold from academic median to production-grade reliability.

concepts.name: Zero-Shot Refactor Assessment
concepts.explanation: Testing whether a single LLM invocation (GPT 5.5 extra high) can complete a substantial refactor without iteration, revealing the gap between declared completion and actual code correctness when it produced only scaffolding with models missing.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates that model self-reported completion does not equal actual task completion, a critical insight for teams evaluating agent autonomy in production refactoring.

concepts.name: AI Psychosis
concepts.explanation: The risk of trusting comprehensive-looking AI deep research reports that describe non-existent features or capabilities, creating false confidence in AI-generated outputs.
concepts.importance: Highlights a novel failure mode specific to AI-assisted development where the surface plausibility of AI output masks substantive gaps, requiring new verification practices.

concepts.name: Agent Harness Evolution
concepts.explanation: Progression of coding agent capabilities through added sub-agents, plan calls, shell commands, and verification steps that reduced manual intervention from O3 to Opus, cutting effort to roughly one-fifth.
concepts.importance: Shows that capability gains come not only from model improvements but from harness sophistication, informing tooling investment decisions for teams building agent workflows.

concepts.name: AI-Native Code Becoming Legacy
concepts.explanation: The risk that code generated by AI degrades into legacy-like patterns with low performance, low quality, and poor developer comprehension if not properly governed.
concepts.importance: Warns that AI-accelerated development can create a new class of technical debt faster than human-written code, making quality governance essential even as velocity increases.

concepts.name: Model Generation Improvement Trajectory
concepts.explanation: The pattern of newer model versions dramatically outperforming predecessors on identical tasks (O3 with 10 mistakes and 3 hours to Opus 4.8 one-shotting the same task at roughly one-fifth the effort).
concepts.importance: Quantifies the rate of improvement that makes the defer-vs-refactor decision a moving target, informing strategic planning for teams evaluating when to invest in AI-assisted engineering.

concepts.name: Monorepo Refactor Strategy
concepts.explanation: Consolidating 10+ legacy repositories into a single monorepo to reduce complexity, improve throughput, and increase developer engagement across teams.
concepts.importance: This is the central engineering decision the entire talk audits. The refactor outcome—faster shipping, lower costs, broader developer participation—demonstrates the monorepo's value in an AI-assisted development context.

concepts.name: Technical Debt as Compounding Financial Debt
concepts.explanation: Framing accumulated code debt as compounding financial debt that worsens exponentially over time if not addressed, motivating proactive refactoring before costs become prohibitive.
concepts.importance: Provides the economic framing that justifies refactoring now rather than deferring indefinitely, connecting software engineering decisions to business outcomes.

concepts.name: Commit Velocity as Refactor Success Metric
concepts.explanation: Using commit frequency and sustained growth as quantitative indicators that a refactor improved developer engagement and codebase health, with the monorepo showing steep, non-flattening commit velocity.
concepts.importance: Offers a measurable, ongoing signal of refactor success beyond initial feature parity, distinguishing a living codebase from a stagnant one.

concepts.name: Feature Parity Verification via Requirements Checklist
concepts.explanation: Systematically verifying the refactored codebase matches all functionality of legacy repos using a requirements checklist, with the team meeting 15 of 17 requirements correctly.
concepts.importance: Provides a concrete, auditable methodology for validating that a refactor preserves business-critical functionality before and after cutover.

concepts.name: Human PR Reviews for Context-Building
concepts.explanation: Using pull request reviews not just for quality control but as a mechanism for building and sharing institutional knowledge during AI-assisted refactoring, with all PR reviews conducted by humans.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates that human review remains essential even in AI-assisted development, serving dual purposes of quality assurance and knowledge transfer.

concepts.name: Plan Mode Adoption in AI Coding Tools
concepts.explanation: Adopting emerging plan-mode features in Claude Code and Cursor to structure agent-driven development workflows as they become available during the refactor lifecycle.
concepts.importance: Shows how teams incrementally integrate new AI tooling capabilities into existing engineering processes rather than adopting everything at once.

concepts.name: Multi-Repo vs Monorepo Trade-offs for AI Development
concepts.explanation: Evaluating differences in sandbox setup, end-to-end testing, and cross-repo navigation between architectures when using AI coding agents, with monorepos simplifying agent navigation but multi-repos remaining viable as models improve.
concepts.importance: Directly informs architectural decisions for teams adopting AI coding tools, as the choice affects agent effectiveness and development workflow.

concepts.name: Refactor-Now vs Defer Decision Framework
concepts.explanation: Framework for deciding whether to refactor immediately or wait for better AI models, weighing current capability ceilings against exponential improvement trends in model performance.
concepts.importance: The core strategic question of the talk—balancing the cost of acting now against the exponentially decreasing cost of waiting—applicable to any team facing legacy modernization.

sections.title: Introduction & Problem Statement
sections.summary: Linkov introduces Wisedocs, which processes complex medical claims as massive PDFs through ML pipelines. Three problems motivate a refactor: slow throughput, pipeline complexity, and developer aversion to touching 10+ legacy repos.

sections.title: Tech Debt & Industry Context
sections.summary: Frames tech debt as compounding financial debt. Cites Anthropic case studies from Spotify and Stripe on AI-accelerated refactoring. Observes that shipping velocity increased industry-wide but product reliability and maintainability degraded, with companies below three-nines uptime.

sections.title: Orchestrator Evaluation & AI Psychosis
sections.summary: Describes 2 months evaluating 5 open-source orchestrators across 17 criteria with POCs. Notes this could now be 90% faster with deep research and sub-agents, but warns of AI psychosis where deep research reports describe non-existent features.

sections.title: Coding Agent Benchmarks on Refactor Task
sections.summary: Benchmarks a Temporal-based refactor task: O3 took 3 hours with 10 major mistakes, Sonnet 4.6 needed one extra iteration, Opus 4.8 essentially one-shot it. Modern harnesses add sub-agents, plan calls, and verifications, reducing manual intervention at ~1/5 original effort.

sections.title: METR Task-Length Curves & Accuracy Thresholds
sections.summary: Argues for reading METR curves at 80-90% success rather than 50%, since coin-flip odds on hour-long runs waste compute and attention. METR preview data shows success declining significantly at the 4-hour mark, with failures even at 15 seconds.

sections.title: Refactor Results & Commit Velocity
sections.summary: Presents results: 10 legacy repos (6+ years old, slow progress) collapsed into a monorepo that reached feature parity within 6 months. Commit velocity was steep and never flattened. Almost every developer now commits to the monorepo even outside their expertise area.

sections.title: Zero-Shot Refactor Experiment: GPT 5.5
sections.summary: Tests whether a modern LLM can zero-shot the entire refactor. GPT 5.5 extra high completed in 10m22s writing 2,000 lines, but produced only scaffolding without actual models. It self-admitted it hadn't added Ray Serve deployment or bootstrap command. Linkov estimates ~6 months until models can consistently complete substantial refactors.

sections.title: Was the Refactor Worthwhile?
sections.summary: Addresses the core question of whether to refactor now or defer for better models. Acknowledges deferring is getting exponentially easier with better models, harnesses, sandboxes, and monitoring. But warns that AI-native code can become legacy-like with low performance and poor understanding. Verdict: yes, the refactor was worthwhile—pipeline time and costs dropped, larger files supported, features shipping in under a week, developers want to work in the codebase, and patterns spread to other repos.

sections.title: Q&A: Multi-Repo Navigation, Requirements, and PR Reviews
sections.summary: During Q&A, Linkov notes models are better at navigating multiple repos now (via folder structures), but end-to-end testing and sandbox setup remain harder. Team got 15 of 17 requirements right during the refactor. Adopted plan mode as it emerged in Claude Code and Cursor. PR reviews were all human during the refactor for context-building, with local skill-based checks, and are continuing to get more autonomous over time.

organization.name: Wisedocs
organization.summary: Wisedocs is an AI-powered automation platform that processes and understands medical documents in real time for the insurance, legal, and medical evaluation industries. Founded in 2018 and headquartered in Toronto, Ontario, Canada, Wisedocs automatically sorts, indexes, summarizes, and reviews unstructured medical documents including PDFs exceeding 10,000 pages. The company employs approximately 111 people and has raised $19.9M in total funding. Clients reportedly benefit from an 85% time reduction and 55% cost reduction in document reviews, and the platform is trained on 100M+ documents and is HIPAA/SOC 2 compliant. The talk features speaker Denys Linkov's audit of Wisedocs' six-month refactor of 10+ legacy medical-claims-processing repositories into a monorepo, including benchmarks of coding agents on the refactor task.

technologies.summary: AI-powered coding assistants (Cursor, Claude Code) benchmarked on a real-world Temporal-based refactor task across model generations. O3 took 3 hours with 10 major mistakes; Sonnet 4.6 needed one additional iteration; Opus 4.8 essentially one-shot the problem at roughly one-fifth original effort. GPT 5.5 extra high zero-shot declared completion in 10m22s writing 2,000 lines, but produced only scaffolding with actual models missing — a self-admitted gap including missing Ray Serve deployment and bootstrap command.
technologies.role: Primary tools benchmarked across model generations on the Temporal refactor task, forming the empirical core of the talk's assessment of AI-assisted refactoring capability

technologies.label: Monorepo Architecture
technologies.summary: Consolidating 10+ legacy medical claims processing repositories (6+ years old) into a single monorepo over 6 months, reaching feature parity with 15 of 17 requirements met correctly. The monorepo showed steep, non-flattening commit velocity, reduced pipeline time and costs, supported larger files, and enabled features that previously took months to ship in under a week. Almost every developer now commits even outside their expertise area, and patterns spread to other repos.
technologies.role: The central engineering decision the entire talk audits — whether refactoring 10+ legacy repos into a monorepo was worthwhile versus deferring for better AI models

technologies.label: METR Task-Length Evaluation
technologies.summary: METR's research framework measuring the time horizon at which AI models complete tasks at given success rates (50% and 80%). Linkov argues for reading curves at 80-90% success rather than the standard 50%, since launching hour-long agent runs on coin-flip odds wastes compute and attention. The 50% horizon doubles roughly every seven months across 12 frontier models, grounding the strategic decision of whether to refactor now or defer for better models.
technologies.role: Provides the analytical framework Linkov uses to assess when AI will be capable enough to consistently complete substantial refactors, directly informing the refactor-now-vs-defer decision

technologies.label: Agent Harness Architecture
technologies.summary: The evolution of coding agent harnesses that added sub-agents, plan calls, shell commands, and verification steps, reducing manual intervention from O3 to Opus and cutting total effort to roughly one-fifth. Plan mode was adopted as it emerged in Claude Code and Cursor during the refactor lifecycle. The talk demonstrates that capability gains come not only from model improvements but from harness sophistication, informing tooling investment decisions for teams building agent workflows.
technologies.role: The harness evolution that reduced manual intervention from O3 to Opus, demonstrating that tooling investment matters as much as model improvement for practical AI-assisted refactoring

challengeSeeds: Build a controlled refactor benchmark: give learners a small legacy multi-repo codebase and ask them to run a coding agent one-shot, then iteratively, and score the output against a requirements checklist (analogous to the 15-of-17 result)

Zero-shot trap challenge: present an AI-generated codebase that declares completion but contains only scaffolding; learners must identify all missing implementations without being told what to look for

METR threshold reasoning challenge: given METR task-length data for several models, ask learners to compute the expected wasted compute at 50% vs 80% thresholds for run costs of $X and argue which threshold to adopt
Refactor-now-or-defer challenge: present a real legacy codebase with known tech debt and a METR doubling-time trend; learners must produce a quantitative recommendation with a timeline and justify it
AI-native legacy detection: provide code samples generated by an LLM and ask learners to identify markers of low performance, low quality, and poor developer comprehensibility
